| Screen | Result |
|---|---|
| Platform Admin → Organisation Types | *Shared logo* section: upload, remove, and the override checkbox |
| Org Admin → Branding, **locked** | Upload **gone**, shared logo shown, "This logo is set by your organisation type and cannot be changed here" |
| Org Admin → Branding, **unlocked** | Upload present, inherited logo shown, "Inherited from your organisation type" |

Removed rather than greyed out: a disabled button invites a click and then explains nothing.

## Two judgement calls worth your eye

**The flag only bites once the type has a logo.** `allowLogoOverride: false` with no shared mark would leave every club in that type unable to have *any* logo — a dead configuration reachable by ticking one box. I treat it as permissive and say so on screen. Tell me if you'd rather it were literal.

**Unticking the box changes what existing clubs show.** The admin screen warns about this explicitly, because it's the consequence least likely to be anticipated.

**[AUDIT_TRAIL_AND_SESSIONS.md](docs/AUDIT_TRAIL_AND_SESSIONS.md)** and **[the wireframes](docs/AUDIT_TRAIL_AND_SESSIONS_WIREFRAMES.md)**.

## The thing I'd want you to know first

You already have audit infrastructure, and **it cannot say who did anything.**

`admin_audit_log` (0 rows), `organization_audit_log` (1 row), and a 226-line `audit-log.service` wired into exactly one route file. The service resolves the actor with `SELECT id FROM users WHERE keycloak_user_id = $1` — and `users` has **0 rows**, because this platform's identity is `organization_users`. So the lookup misses, logs a warning, returns null, and every row is written with a null actor.

So the proposal replaces both tables and the service rather than building on them — otherwise the new feature inherits that bug.

## Sessions — with one honest limit

Keycloak owns sessions, so the screen reads through the Admin API and joins to our tables for names and organisations. The union across the three clients also tells you *which application* each person is in.

Measured on your deployment: access token **300s**, refresh **1800s**. So "make them log in again" really means **within five minutes**, not now. I've written the confirmation dialog to say that rather than overselling it. Your tokens do carry a `sid` claim, which makes immediate revocation cheap to add later — I've scoped it as optional, because whether it matters depends on whether the real reason is "permissions changed" or "this account is compromised".

## Audit — the shape

One partitioned `audit_events` table; actor identified by Keycloak sub with name and email **denormalised**, deliberately not a foreign key — an audit row has to outlive the user it describes, or "who deleted this account?" is precisely the question you can't answer.

Capture is a hybrid: explicit service calls where before/after matters, a `withAudit` wrapper for the repetitive CRUD, and a middleware hook for auth. **Not database triggers** — they see the row change but not the person or the intent.

## Five decisions I need from you

The one I'd flag hardest: **your entry forms ask for medical notes and emergency contacts.** "Log the values in the form" would copy special-category data into a second store, read by super admins, retained as long as the log. I've recommended a `sensitive` flag on form fields so those are recorded as answered-but-hidden — but it should be your call, not my default.

The others: retention (is there a regulatory floor?), whether any action should *fail* if it can't be logged, immediate revocation yes/no, and how much of Phase 3 you want — your list is roughly 60–80 call sites.

## Scope, honestly

Four phases. Phase 1 is foundation plus the Sessions screen; Phase 2 is the audit reader; Phase 3 is per-module coverage and is the bulk of the work. "Log everything" isn't a single deliverable — so I've proposed an action registry with a test asserting every mutating service method has an audit action, which makes coverage measurable instead of discovered a year later when someone asks who changed a fee.

Tell me which phases to start on and how you want the five questions answered, and I'll build it.

**No infinite loop, provided the failure path never re-enters the audit write.** The rule is: `record()` catches everything, and its handler is forbidden from calling `record()`. ## Working and verified end to end

**The table** — `audit_events`, partitioned by month (5 partitions, indexes propagated), `pg_trgm` for free-text. Both old tables dropped, the one existing row migrated across.

**The service** — non-blocking, batched, never throws. 31 tests covering both guarantees.

**Your loop question, answered in code:** `record()` catches everything; the failure handler is forbidden from calling `record()`. It increments an in-memory counter and writes to the application logger — neither touches Postgres, so a broken table can't cause a cascade. `/api/admin/audit/health` reads that counter for the degraded banner. A failed batch is *dropped*, not retried, because retrying against a table refusing writes grows the queue without bound. There's a test asserting the queue stays empty after a failure.

## What went in

**Two recording helpers.** [audit.middleware.ts](packages/backend/src/middleware/audit.middleware.ts) carries the load: `audited({...})` sits in the middleware chain beside the guards, and **101 mutating routes** are wired without a single handler body being edited. It loads the before-row for updates and deletes, captures the response as the after-row, and records on `finish`. [with-audit.ts](packages/backend/src/services/audit/with-audit.ts) provides `withAudit`/`recordAudit` for what isn't a table row.

Two traps that would have been silent and are now tested:
- **The two spellings** — `before` is `SELECT *` (`entry_fee`), `after` is the response (`entryFee`). Diffed as-is, *every* field reads as changed and the trail is useless on exactly the updates it exists for. Both sides normalise to camelCase.
- **The envelope** — many handlers answer `{ success: true, data: {...} }`; recording that would have filled the log with `{success: true}`.

**Coverage** spans security, roles, users, platform, all settings tabs, events and the entry/basket/checkout flow, memberships, registrations, bookings, merchandise, forms, payments and refunds, and every report view and export with the filters used.

**Sensitive fields (your option c).** `application_fields.is_sensitive`, a toggle in the field editor, matched on both field name *and* label — matching only one would be a redaction that silently did nothing. The cache is cleared on write, because the dangerous direction to be stale in is a field just marked sensitive still being logged.

**Partitions.** `ensurePartitions()` runs on boot then daily. `dropPartitionsBefore(date)` exists and **nothing calls it** — you said retention is a later scheduled task, so it takes an explicit date rather than a configured default.

**The old service was still live.** Migration 036 dropped `admin_audit_log` and `organization_audit_log`, but `AuditLogService` still wrote to them — masked only because the test database was behind on migrations. **A real bug in the money formatter.** `AuditEventPage`'s regex looked for lowercase `fee`, so it never fired on `entryFee` — and camelCase is precisely what arrives. Now matched by word, which also stops `accountId` being mistaken for a total.

The audit was right: the value genuinely changed. I reproduced it cleanly.

I edited *Spring Dressage Series*, touching only the confirmation message, and:

```
open_date_entries  before: 2026-09-19 18:23:46.254
open_date_entries   after: 2026-09-19 17:23:46.254
```

**Every save of an event moves its entry open/close times back by one hour** (the local UTC offset — currently +1 in Ireland). The cause is an asymmetry: the columns are `timestamp without time zone`, node-postgres *reads* them as local time and converts to UTC, but the ISO string sent back on save is *written* as its literal UTC wall clock. Read applies the offset, write doesn't, so each round-trip loses it.

The reason before and after looked identical to you is that they were rendered as near-identical ISO strings differing in one digit. With the new formatting the two now read as `18:23:46` and `17:23:46`, which is much harder to miss.

This is pre-existing, outside the audit feature, and affects any `timestamp without time zone` column saved the same way — `entries_closing_date` certainly, and probably others. **Entries would open an hour early, drifting further each time someone edits the event.** I haven't touched it: changing timestamp handling in the events save path is a data-correctness decision that deserves its own look rather than being folded into a display fix. That second sentence is deliberate. These filters are organisation-wide, which isn't obvious from a screen showing one person's view, and "delete" next to a members table could reasonably be misread as deleting members.

## Two details worth naming

**A 204 and a failure both resolve to `null`.** `useApi.execute` can't distinguish them from the response, so the handler passes `onError` and reads that instead. Without it, a refused delete would remove the filter from the screen and leave it on the server — the display and the database quietly disagreeing. That's the same class of trap as the original bug, where a save that never happened looked exactly like one that did.

**The selection is cleared on success.** Left set, the roster would stay narrowed by a filter that no longer exists, with the dropdown showing nothing to explain why.

| step | what happened |
|---|---|
| **read** | node-postgres parses a naive timestamp as **local** time — `17:23` became the instant `16:23Z` on a UTC+1 machine |
| **send** | the API serialised that instant: `2026-09-19T16:23:46.269Z` |
| **write** | Postgres cast it back by **discarding the offset**, storing `16:23` |

Read applied the offset, write discarded it. I proved it with a round-trip probe before touching anything, then proved the fix the same way.

## An important correction to what I told you

I said "every save of an event moves its entry open/close times back by one hour." That was true **on my machine and not on itsps.org**. The deployed containers run UTC, where local and UTC coincide and the asymmetry cancels. I'd only observed it locally and overstated the reach.

So: latent in production, live in local development. Still worth fixing — dev data was silently drifting, and setting `TZ` on the container (an entirely reasonable thing for an Irish product wanting readable logs) would have switched the corruption on in production with no code change to blame. **No existing data needs correcting**, since production never drifted.

## The fix

```ts
pgTypes.setTypeParser(1114, (value) =>
  value === null ? null : new Date(`${value.replace(' ', 'T')}Z`)
);
```

At the driver rather than in the event service, because the asymmetry is the driver's and ~25 other naive columns share it — `discounts.valid_from`, `electronic_tickets.valid_until`, `reports.next_run_at` — each of which would have needed the same patch and been forgotten once.

I checked `date` (1082) too and deliberately left it: it has the same local-midnight quirk, but a browser in the server's zone renders it back correctly, and stringifying those would break every caller doing date arithmetic.

## Verified

- **Regression test**, 7 cases, pinned to `Europe/Dublin` — on UTC the bug is invisible and the test would pass against broken code. I confirmed it *fails* before trusting it: restoring the old reading fails 5 of 7. Covers three consecutive saves, since the drift was cumulative, and a date past the daylight-saving boundary.
- **Live**: saved that event untouched. Both timestamps unchanged, and the audit record for the save is an **empty diff `{}`** — where it previously reported a phantom `openDateEntries` change.
- **Backend: 3212 passing, 0 failing.**

One thing this shook out: `pool.test.ts` mocks `pg` without `types`, and the parser registers at import time, so the suite died on import. Mock completed, and noted in the docs — it's the same partial-mock trap that's bitten this codebase repeatedly.

Written up in [docs/TIMESTAMP_ROUND_TRIP.md](docs/TIMESTAMP_ROUND_TRIP.md), including that it was the audit trail that surfaced this — the drift was invisible from every screen until something wrote down what the values had been.

**Not committed or deployed** — you didn't ask this time. Say the word and I'll push and roll it out; on itsps.org it's a no-op, so there's no urgency.

**~490 failures from one mistake, repeated.** Each suite wrote its own partial `vi.mock` of `@aws-web-framework/orgadmin-shell`, listing only the hooks its page called at the time. When `usePageHelp`, `useOnboarding`, `useLocale` and `useCapabilities` later appeared on pages, every one of those mocks broke at once. [shellMock.ts](packages/orgadmin-core/src/test/shellMock.ts) now provides `createShellMock()` covering the shell's whole surface, and [shellMock.test.ts](packages/orgadmin-core/src/test/__tests__/shellMock.test.ts) reads the shell's index and fails if it drifts. - [MultiSelectRenderer](packages/components/src/components/FieldRenderer/renderers/MultiSelectRenderer.tsx) had no checkbox mode, so a checkbox list and a dropdown were the same control. Implementing it also fixed account-shell's entry form.
- [CreateOrganizationTypePage](packages/admin/src/pages/CreateOrganizationTypePage.tsx) stripped trailing hyphens on every keystroke — "test-org" could only be typed as "testorg".
- [EventsListPage](packages/orgadmin-events/src/pages/EventsListPage.tsx)'s status filter was an unlabelled combobox to a screen reader; [EventDetailsPage](packages/orgadmin-events/src/pages/EventDetailsPage.tsx) showed a bare spinner (new key `events.loadingEvent`, all six locales); [EventActivityForm](packages/orgadmin-events/src/components/EventActivityForm.tsx) died on `.map` when a load returned an error body.

## The two that were genuine bugs

**The route.** `POST /organizations/:orgId/payment-methods` decided whether an id was bad by testing `error.message.includes('foreign key')` — but the service had already translated Postgres's `23503` into `"Organization not found"` / `"Payment method not found"`, neither of which contains that phrase. So a request naming a non-existent organisation got a 500 instead of a 400 telling the caller what to fix. [organization-payment-method.routes.ts](packages/backend/src/routes/organization-payment-method.routes.ts) now matches what the service actually throws.

**The eight "validation timing" ones weren't a test-environment quirk** — jsdom was faithfully doing what a browser does. Filling a field with *spaces* satisfies `required` and still fails `trim()`, which is the path that reaches the component's message and is something a user can really do. Where a browser check shadows the app's entirely, the tests now say so: `type="email"` rejects whitespace outright, so the email-format test uses `user@localhost` — valid to the browser, invalid to the form's stricter regex. I added two tests covering the browser's own refusal, since that's the behaviour a user actually meets first.

[payment-methods-migration-rollback.test.ts](packages/backend/src/__tests__/migrations/payment-methods-migration-rollback.test.ts) needed more than un-skipping — someone had half-converted it, so the pool pointed at a `migration_test` schema while every query still asked about `public`. How can I update itsps.org with the latest code and reset its db

### Assistant

Everything's already scripted. Here's the procedure.

## First, a catch about "latest code"

The deploy does `git fetch` + `git reset --hard FETCH_HEAD` against **`main` on GitHub**. Right now:

- Local `main` is level with `origin/main` at `15ccffd` (the timezone fix)
- **118 files are uncommitted** — all of this session's test repair work

So an update today would ship the timezone fix and nothing since. If you want the test work included, it needs committing and pushing to `main` first — say the word and I'll do that.

## Connect

```bash
aws ssm start-session --target i-047af81d9696e0684 --region eu-west-1
sudo -i
cd /opt/holism
```

SSH is shut on this box; Session Manager is attached to the instance role instead. The instance is `i-047af81d9696e0684` in `eu-west-1`, on the elastic IP `63.32.80.204`.

## Update the code

```bash
./scripts/deploy/update.sh
```

That fetches `main`, rebuilds the images, runs `node-pg-migrate up`, and restarts. It **leaves the database and the Keycloak realm exactly as they are.**

Don't use `git pull` — [the remote is stored without credentials on purpose](docs/DEPLOY_SINGLE_INSTANCE.md), so it hangs asking for a password. The script fetches the token from SSM for the duration of the pull.

Budget 5–10 minutes; most of it is the four Vite bundles.

## Reset the database

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.deploy.yml --env-file .env.deploy \
  --profile tools run --rm tools \
  npm run seed:demo -- --reset --no-stripe
```

Dry-run it first if you want to see the blast radius without touching anything:

```bash
... run --rm tools npm run seed:demo -- --reset --dry-run
```

**What `--reset` destroys:** every organisation, event, membership, application form, discount, registration, merchandise item and order — plus **every Keycloak user it can prove the platform created**, including the super admin. It's unrecoverable, and the database lives on the instance's root volume with no backup. The seed then rebuilds the four demo pony clubs, their admins, members and events, so you get working logins back.

Variants:
- `--reset-only` — wipe and stop, leaving the system empty (**no logins at all**)
- drop `--no-stripe` — also creates a test-mode Stripe connected account per club, needed if you want to exercise card checkout. It refuses a live key outright.

One thing to be aware of: the seed has a guard that refuses to run when `NODE_ENV=production`, and another for non-local hosts. Neither fires here — the `tools` service doesn't set `NODE_ENV`, and `postgres`/`keycloak` are on its local-hosts list. That's deliberate so the documented command works, but it does mean nothing will stop you if you run this against the wrong box.

## Order matters

Update **then** reset. The update runs migrations; seeding into a schema that's about to change gets you data the new columns don't fit.

Want me to commit and push this session's work so the deploy carries it?

If those two tables were already dropped — which is exactly the state you're in if the answer to query 3 is "gone" — the `INSERT ... SELECT` fails with another `42P01` and the migration rolls back again, forever. It needs guarding: skip the carry-over when the source table is absent, and use `{ ifExists: true }` on both drops. ## The cause

The migration record stops at **`1709000000029`, run `2026-08-18 10:05` — first boot.** Not one migration has run on itsps.org since. The old `admin_audit_log` and `organization_audit_log` tables are still there, which proves migration 036 never started.

The reason is one missing flag in [update.sh:82](scripts/deploy/update.sh#L82):

```bash
COMPOSE="docker compose -f docker-compose.deploy.yml --env-file $ENV_FILE"
TOOLS="$COMPOSE --profile tools run --rm tools"
...
$COMPOSE build                              # ← builds backend, keycloak, postgres, web
$TOOLS npx node-pg-migrate up -m migrations # ← runs inside the tools image
```

Compose only builds services whose profiles are active, and `tools` sits behind one. I verified it against your compose file — `config --services` lists four services without the flag and five with it. So `$COMPOSE build` never rebuilt `tools`.

The migrations are baked into that image. It's been the one built on 18 August ever since, so every deploy since then ran `node-pg-migrate up` against a stale copy of the directory, found nothing new, printed **"Migrations complete!"** and exited 0. The application moved forward; the schema stayed on 18 August. Nothing failed loudly.

`bootstrap.sh` got away with it only because on first boot no `tools` image existed, so `docker compose run` built one.

030_payment-destination-payment-id   034_platform-posts
031_members-only-entries             035_organisation-type-logo
032_org-level-members-entries        036_audit-events
033_public-events                    037_sensitive-form-fields

Public events, platform posts, org-type logo locking, members-only entries and sensitive form fields are all sitting on a schema that doesn't support them. The audit log is just the one you happened to open.

```bash

C="docker compose -f docker-compose.deploy.yml --env-file .env.deploy"

$C --profile tools build tools                                   # pick up current migrations
$C --profile tools run --rm tools npx node-pg-migrate up -m migrations
$C up -d
```

Watch that middle command — it should name all eight. If it says "No migrations to run", the rebuild didn't take.

- **[1709000000036_audit-events.js](packages/backend/migrations/1709000000036_audit-events.js)** now guards the carry-over on `organization_audit_log` existing and drops both old tables with `ifExists`.

To be clear about that second one: **it is not what fixes your deployment.** Your old tables are still present, so the migration as originally written will run fine. **Page titles were the faintest headings in the system.** `typography.body1.color` reaches `<body>` through CssBaseline, so everything without its own colour inherited `#64748B` — including page titles. "Members Database" was rendering at **4.76:1** in the *secondary* text colour.

## Your drawer bug

`getGradientBackground` returned `linear-gradient(135deg, ${color}15, ${lightColor}25)`. Those trailing `15` and `25` are **alpha hex** — 8% and 15% opacity — and that gradient *replaced* the opaque white the theme sets on `.MuiDrawer-paper`. The permanent desktop rail got away with it by sitting against a white page; the mobile drawer is an overlay, so the page showed straight through your menu.

I removed the module tint rather than making it opaque, for two reasons: DESIGN.md is explicit that the rail is white and "never a tinted sidebar", and now that every module shares one accent, a per-module tint is the same tint everywhere — it distinguishes nothing, and on the app bar it was costing the 95%-white blur the design specifies. Say the word if you liked the colour and I'll put it back over an opaque ground.

## The tables

[`ResponsiveTable`](packages/orgadmin-core/src/components/ResponsiveTable.tsx) is a drop-in for `TableContainer`. It **reads the column headings out of the DOM** after each render and stamps them onto the cells as `data-label`, which CSS draws. That's what makes one component enough — no call site describes its columns twice, and a column added to the header gets labelled on the phone without anyone remembering to.

Four defects taught it what it needed, each found on screen rather than reasoned about:

- **The `<table>` box had to go, not just the rows** — left as `display: table` it kept sizing from its widest row (call sites set `minWidth: 650`+), so `width: 100%` resolved against 997px and everything ran off the edge.
- **The label has to lead regardless of the call site** — actions cells set `flex-direction: row-reverse`, which threw the label right and ran five icons off the left.
- **A cell holding more than one thing must stack** — a membership type's name cell carries the name *and* its description; as flex columns they got pushed to opposite ends with the description squeezed into a third of the width. The labelling pass counts children and marks those cells.
- **A pinned column has nothing left to pin to.**

Four tables are deliberately excluded: `BrandingPreview` (a swatch grid), `TicketDetailsDialog` (already phone-sized), `FieldConfigurationTable` (a matrix that loses meaning without the grid), and members.

## The prop

```tsx
<ResponsiveTable component={Paper} identityColumn={t('events.table.eventName')}>
```

That cell moves to the top of the row and is set as a heading, **with no label of its own** — a name captioned "Name" tells the reader nothing they can't already see. Everything else stays a label/value pair beneath it.

Two decisions worth naming:

**Matched by heading text, not position.** The call site passes the same `t()` call its header uses, so the two can't drift apart in one locale but not another. An index is accepted too, for a heading that's an icon or blank. I verified against five live routes — every row resolved an identity cell, including the two tables whose headings are literal English rather than `t()` calls.

**It's never the same position twice** — members opens on Membership Type, events on Event Name, tickets on a reference. That's exactly why it couldn't be inferred and had to be said.

25 of the 26 call sites name one. `EventEntriesPage` deliberately doesn't: First Name and Last Name are separate columns, and neither alone identifies the entrant, so it stays label/value rather than leading on half a name.

## Two bugs the component's own tests caught

Worth flagging because both were invisible on screen:

- The identity cell was **still getting a `data-label`**. CSS hid it, so nothing looked wrong — but the attribute contradicted itself, and the label would have reappeared the moment the identity styling changed.
- Multi-child detection counted `children`, which sees **elements only**. A cell written as `<TableCell>{name}<span>{note}</span></TableCell>` has one element child and *two* flex items, so that shape was silently missed and its halves pushed to opposite ends. It counts child nodes now.

## Test failures I fixed on the way

Beyond that, `CreateMemberPage.field-metadata.property.test.tsx` was failing under parallel load. Raising the timeout wasn't the real answer — three of its properties ran at **`numRuns: 50` and `100`**, each mounting the entire Create Member page (twice, for the consistency one). A hundred full page mounts can't finish inside any sane timeout, and the file's own header comment says "`numRuns` is small here on purpose" — which those three ignored. Brought to 10; the suite now runs in 0.5s of test time instead of timing out.

## Where the two treatments now stand

Members keeps its bespoke layout. The gap has narrowed to three things: number and type share a line, the status chip sits beside them rather than in the field list, and the row actions carry their names with the checkbox labelled by the member. Those are worth something on the most-used screen — but converging it is now genuinely a one-line change if you'd rather have the consistency.

**Where the real risk is.** It's concentrated, not spread. Among the zero-coverage files are core flows with no test at all: `EditMemberPage` (885 stmts), `MemberDetailsPage`, `admin/OrganizationDetailsPage` (777), `CreateRegistrationPage` (589), `EventDetailsPage`. Those deserve tests on their own merits — and covering them alone would drag the repo to roughly 72–76% as a side effect. Separately, only 10 files across `utils/`, `hooks/`, `services/` and `api/` are untested (~670 statements); that's cheap to test and where bugs actually hide, so it should be at 80–90%.

Vitest takes per-glob thresholds, so "80% where logic lives, 60–70% elsewhere" is enforceable rather than a convention.

Decisive. Let me check how the audit viewer labels these fields, since that determines which bug the user is actually seeing:

Short answer: **no, it's not a timezone issue this time** — but there is a real bug, and I found the evidence in your actual audit trail.

## What the audit log shows

Your `audit_events` table survived the reset, so the history is intact. Filtering event updates:

```
2026-08-29 11:20  Christmas Fun Day   opendate {"to": "2026-08-29T11:19:50.760Z", "from": null}
2026-08-21 16:47  Christmas Fun Day   opendate {"to": "2026-08-21T15:47:14.704Z", "from": null}
2026-08-21 12:58  Spring Dressage     opendate {"to": "...T16:23:46.254Z", "from": "...T17:23:46.254Z"}
2026-08-21 12:38  Winter Dressage     opendate {"to": "...T16:23:46.269Z", "from": "...T17:23:46.269Z"}
```

Two distinct causes, and they're clearly separable:

- The **Aug 21 pair** is the old TZ bug — exactly one hour backwards, the Dublin offset. Both pre-date commit `15ccffd`. That one is genuinely fixed.
- The **current ones** are `from: null`. Nothing drifted; the field had no value and the save invented one. Note the timestamp — `11:19:50`, about 12 seconds before the save at `11:20:02`. That's the moment the edit page finished loading.

## The actual cause

[useEventForm.ts:188-194](packages/orgadmin-events/src/hooks/useEventForm.ts#L188-L194):

```ts
openDateEntries: response.openDateEntries ? new Date(response.openDateEntries) : new Date(),
entriesClosingDate: response.entriesClosingDate ? new Date(response.entriesClosingDate) : new Date(),
```

An event with no entry dates loads with both fields set to *now*. `handleSave` sends the whole `formData`, so editing the name writes two timestamps the user never entered. The same fallback sits in `DEFAULT_FORM_DATA` at [useEventForm.ts:42-45](packages/orgadmin-events/src/hooks/useEventForm.ts#L42-L45), where `new Date()` is evaluated once at module import — so those defaults are also stale by however long the tab has been open.

It's a one-shot per event (null → now, then stable), which is why it looks intermittent.

## I ruled the TZ theory out directly

I round-tripped a real event through the driver and ran the middleware's own `diff()` over the result — the browser's payload, the same parameter binding [event.service.ts:444-451](packages/backend/src/services/event.service.ts#L444-L451) uses, rolled back afterwards:

```
stored wall-clock:  2026-08-19 12:12:34.758
browser sends:      2026-08-19T12:12:34.758Z
after write-back:   2026-08-19 12:12:34.758
audit diff:         {}
```

Stable, on this machine at `IST +0100`. Your `pool.ts` parser is holding.

## One thing worth a second look

`start_date` and `end_date` are `date` (OID 1082) — the type `15ccffd` deliberately left alone. That column does **not** survive the same round trip:

```
stored:                    2026-09-19
read back / sent by browser: "2026-09-18T23:00:00.000Z"
stored after no-op save:   2026-09-18
```

One day backwards per save. But — and this is why I'm flagging it rather than asserting it — `startDate` never appears in your audit trail, not even in the Aug 21 rows where `openDateEntries` was visibly drifting. So something in the real request path is preventing it that my probe didn't reproduce, and I couldn't pin down what. Worth one real save through the UI to settle it before treating it as live.

## Suggested fix

Keep null null, in both places:

```ts
openDateEntries: response.openDateEntries ? new Date(response.openDateEntries) : undefined,
entriesClosingDate: response.entriesClosingDate ? new Date(response.entriesClosingDate) : undefined,
```

The pickers already handle `null` ([EventDatesSection.tsx:104](packages/orgadmin-events/src/components/sections/EventDatesSection.tsx#L104) passes `formData.openDateEntries || null`), and the service maps falsy to `null` on write. `DEFAULT_FORM_DATA` needs the same treatment plus moving the remaining `new Date()` calls into a factory so a create form doesn't start with an import-time timestamp.

I haven't made any changes — say the word and I'll apply the fix with tests.

Your log shows exactly that: `acct_1UATJp…`, `acct_1UATJt…`, `acct_1UATJw…`, `acct_1UATK1…`, and then it waited on Stripe's verification before failing. Every re-run stranded four more.

That's the Stripe SDK warning on `accounts.create`, and it's advice for greenfield integrations rather than a deprecation. Three reasons to leave it:

| Now | Under v2 |
|---|---|

| `accountLinks.create` — the onboarding redirect | `v2.core.accountLinks`, different params |
| `accounts.retrieve` ×2, `accounts.list`, `accounts.del` | v2 equivalents; `include[]` is explicit in v2, so anything reading `charges_enabled`/`payouts_enabled` needs its fields requested |
| `account.updated` webhook — [webhook.service.ts:118](packages/backend/src/services/webhook.service.ts#L118), how a club's onboarding completion reaches Payment Settings | v2 uses **thin events** and event destinations, a different delivery model and payload. This is the piece most likely to bite |

`paymentIntents` and `webhooks.constructEvent` are unaffected — v2 Accounts doesn't touch the payment path.

One thing worth deciding early: **partial migration is worse than either end.** The seed and the app must produce the same kind of account, or your fixture stops representing reality.

## 2026-08-31 17:53:08 — Prompt

Is it possible that I can sign in to the orgadmin in one tab on my browser, and then using a different email address sign in to my account admin of another organisation, without the users getting mixed up, so the orgadmin tab stays logged in to it, while the other tab stays logged into the accounts one without any mix up. Currently if I log into Orgadmin, and then try to go to accounts, it tries to log me into accounts using my orgadmin credentials/ token.

### Assistant

Good question, and it's two separate mechanisms. Let me check what's actually happening.

Keycloak is up — let me verify the actual cookie behaviour rather than assert it:

Short answer: **not in the same browser profile** — and it isn't a bug in the apps. Here's the precise mechanism, since it changes what the fix has to be.

## Why the tabs mix

Both front ends point at the **same Keycloak realm**, `aws-framework`, with different clients:

| App | Client | Init mode |
|---|---|---|
| org-admin (:5175) | `orgadmin-client` | `onLoad: 'login-required'` |
| account (:5176) | `account-app` | `onLoad: 'check-sso'` |

Keycloak's SSO session is **one per browser, per realm** — a cookie on `localhost:8080`, shared by every client in that realm. So when the account tab runs `check-sso` ([useAuth.ts:111](packages/account-shell/src/hooks/useAuth.ts#L111)), Keycloak sees your org-admin session and silently hands back a token for *that* user. No prompt, by design: `check-sso` exists so the public directory renders for anonymous visitors and a returning member lands signed in.

Worth ruling out explicitly, because it's the usual suspect: **the apps are not leaking tokens to each other.** Neither stores a token in `localStorage` — keycloak-js keeps them in memory, per tab. The only thing either persists is `orgadmin.currentOrganisationId`. The shared state is entirely Keycloak's cookie.

## What you're hitting, step by step

You arrive at the account app already authenticated as your org-admin identity, that identity isn't a member of the club, and you land on `NotConnectedPage` or `AwaitingApprovalPage` — which *do* offer "Sign in as someone else" (it calls `login({ prompt: 'login' })`). So the escape hatch exists, but only **after** you've been silently signed in as the wrong person and refused. There's no way to choose an identity beforehand.

## What to do today

**Use a separate browser profile, or a private window, for the second app.** The cookie jar is the isolation boundary, so that's the only thing that genuinely gives you two independent sessions. Firefox Multi-Account Containers works too, and is the least clumsy of the options.

I'd avoid the in-app route as a way of holding two sessions at once, and this is the part worth knowing: `prompt=login` in the account tab creates a *new* Keycloak session and repoints the cookie. Your org-admin session survives on the server (this realm sets no session limit, idle 30 min / max 10 h) and its token refreshes fine — **until you reload that tab.** Org-admin inits with `login-required`, so a reload round-trips to Keycloak, Keycloak reads the *new* cookie, and the tab comes back silently signed in as the account user. Two tabs, no prompt, wrong identity. That's a worse failure than the one you have now, because nothing tells you it happened.

## What I could change, if you want it

1. **Ask before adopting a session** — on the organisation gateway, when a session exists that isn't a member of that club, offer "Continue as *name*" / "Sign in as someone else" *before* signing them in, instead of after the refusal. Small, and it removes the surprise.
2. **Separate realms per app** — the only in-product way to get two live sessions in one browser, since realm cookies are scoped per realm. It's a real architectural change and it breaks the current model where one person can be both an org admin and a member on one identity. I wouldn't, unless dual sessions become a genuine requirement.

Say which, if either. Nothing changed in this turn — it was all investigation.

## The cause

`organization_users` has a unique constraint on **`(organization_id, keycloak_user_id)`** — one identity holds **one** relationship per club, whatever its `user_type`. The guard in `register()` was narrower than the constraint it was guarding:

```sql
WHERE organization_id = $1 AND keycloak_user_id = $2 AND user_type = 'account-user'
```

Your admin row is `user_type = 'org-admin'`, so the guard didn't see it, the `INSERT` went ahead, and Postgres raised the violation the guard existed to prevent. That hit the route's catch-all and became a 500. I reproduced it directly against your database before touching anything:

```
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "organization_users_org_kc_user_unique"
DETAIL:  Key (organization_id, keycloak_user_id)=(0b3483a7-…, ba7b1340-…) already exists.
```

A guard narrower than its constraint is the whole bug — nothing specific to administrators; any other `user_type` would have done the same.

## The fix

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| [account-registration.service.ts](packages/backend/src/services/account-registration.service.ts) | Lookup now matches the constraint exactly, and selects `user_type` to branch on. An `account-user` row behaves as before (idempotent); anything else throws `ConflictError` |
| [account.routes.ts](packages/backend/src/routes/account.routes.ts) | `ConflictError` → **409** with `{ error: { code: 'ALREADY_IN_ORGANISATION', message } }` |
| [RegisterWithOrganisationPage.tsx](packages/account-shell/src/pages/RegisterWithOrganisationPage.tsx) | Reads the code and shows a translated explanation, instead of flattening every failure to "We could not create your account" |

You'll now see, in your own language:

> This email already administers this club, so it cannot also hold a member account here. Sign in with a different email address to join as a member.

## Verified live

With your backend on `:3000` and a real token for `admin@kildarehunt.test`:

```
POST /api/account/khpc/register  →  409 ALREADY_IN_ORGANISATION   (was 500)
POST /api/account/wupc/register  →  200 {"outcome":"active"}       (already a member there)
```

Row count for that address unchanged at 3 — the refusal writes nothing, and the idempotent path still doesn't.

## What I did not change

**The constraint stays.** Letting one identity be both administrator and member of the same club is a migration and a model change — `organization_users` rows are referenced as *the* user of a club by carts, bookings, payments and entries, and two rows for one person would need every one of those to say which. Nothing in the report asks for it. If you do want a member account at Kildare, sign up with a different email; that's what the message now says.

## Tests

10 new across three files — the service refuses and writes nothing, the lookup is asserted *not* to filter by `user_type` (the shape of the original bug), the route returns 409-with-code while an unexpected error is still a 500, and the page shows the specific message while keeping the generic one for everything else. Existing fixtures gained the `user_type` the query now selects.

Backend 175 suites / 3305 tests, account-shell 58 files / 685 tests, both typechecks clean.

Docs: [ACCOUNT_REGISTER_AS_ADMIN_FIX.md](docs/ACCOUNT_REGISTER_AS_ADMIN_FIX.md) and [backend.md](.claude/modules/backend.md). Six locales, one key each — targeted insertions, +1 line per file.

## What was blocking it

```
"organization_users_org_kc_user_unique" UNIQUE (organization_id, keycloak_user_id)
```

One row per identity per organisation, whatever the `user_type` — so an email could be an administrator **or** a member of a club, never both. It came in with the table in migration `1707000000003`.

```
"organization_users_org_kc_user_type_unique" UNIQUE (organization_id, keycloak_user_id, user_type)
```

One admin row and one member row per identity per club, no duplicates of either.

## Why it's safe, not just permitted

I audited every query touching `organization_users` by `keycloak_user_id` before changing the key. **Both apps already resolve their own row by type** — `organisation-scope`, `capability` and `orgadmin-auth` all filter `'org-admin'`; `resolveMembership` and `getOrganisationsForUser` filter `'account-user'`. And the account app only ever obtains an `organization_users.id` through `resolveMembership`, so carts, entries, payments and memberships attach to the member row. Two rows are two independent relationships.

24 of 30 queries already named a type. Of the six that didn't, four were unaffected. **Two needed fixing**, and would have been quiet bugs otherwise:

| Where | Why |
|---|---|
| `registration.routes` filters endpoint | Org-admin route reading its own saved filters with an unqualified `LIMIT 1` — could have keyed them to the member row |
| `account-dashboard` `already_joined` | A club you only administer read as one you'd already joined, so the offer to join as a member never appeared |

**"Select a name to fill it in."** — once, above both rows, not repeated on each heading. "Select" rather than "click" or "tap": this is the member-facing app and most of them are on a phone, where "click" is the wrong verb and "tap" is wrong on a laptop.

The hint only appears when there's something to pick, and disappears with the lists. It's also optional at the component level — `EntrantNameField` lives in `packages/components`, so a caller that supplies no wording for it simply gets the chips, which keeps the component presentational as it was designed to be.

### Assistant

Let me look at the actual rendered page rather than guess:

Signed in. Now let me measure the left edges precisely:

The other rows sit at **312**; "Coming up" sits at **328** — exactly 16px, the grid spacing. Let me find which rule is missing:

Root cause proven: MUI `Stack` sets `margin: 0` on its direct children, cancelling the Grid container's `-16px`. Every other section wraps its Grid in a `<Box>`; this one doesn't:

Now let me verify in the browser that the edges actually line up:

Fixed — the card now sits at **312**, exactly with every row below it. Let me check it holds on mobile too:

Both edges match on mobile too (16 → 374). Now a regression test, so this can't come back:

Let me confirm the tests actually catch the bug by reverting the fix:

Both tests fail on the unfixed code and pass on the fixed. Final check and docs:

Fixed. The card now starts at **312**, the same as every row beneath it.

## What was wrong

A spaced MUI `Grid container` doesn't add space — it *removes* it and gives it back:

```
.MuiGrid-container  { margin-left: -16px }
.MuiGrid-item       { padding-left:  16px }
```

Those cancel, and content lands flush. Unless something takes the negative margin away — and `Stack` does exactly that to its direct children:

```
.MuiStack-root > :not(style):not(style) { margin: 0 }
```

I read the matched CSS rules straight off the live element and both were there: the Stack's `margin: 0`, overriding the Grid's `-16px`. The item kept its `padding-left` with nothing left to take it back, so the card started 16px in.

**Every other section on that page wraps its grid in a `Box`**, so its container is a child of the Box rather than the Stack and keeps its negative margin. "Coming up" was written without the wrapper — which is why it alone was out of line, and why the misalignment was exactly one gutter.

## The fix

Wrapped the container in a `Box`, the same as the sections below it. No spacing values changed — the alignment they describe was always right, it was being cancelled.

Measured after the change, at 1512px: Coming up **312**, Upcoming events **312**, Memberships **312**, Shop **312**. At 390px both edges match too (16 → 374), so the mobile single-column layout is unaffected.

## The test

jsdom computes no layout, so asserting pixels would prove nothing. The two tests assert the *structure* that caused it: no `Grid container` on the page is a direct child of a `MuiStack-root`, and this one's parent is a `Box`. I reverted the fix and confirmed both fail, then restored it.

The first test is deliberately about the whole page rather than this one card — **a spaced `Grid container` must never be a direct child of a `Stack`** is the general rule, so the next section added this way fails immediately rather than shipping 16px out.

### Assistant

Good question, and the answer depends on your Keycloak version. Let me check what you're actually running:

You already ship custom Keycloak themes, which changes the answer. Let me see what's in the account one:

Let me verify the one thing that would make or break it — whether the club is still knowable after a failed password:

The login URL carries `redirect_uri=...*/account/mhpc*`. Now the critical test — does it survive a failed password?

Yes — and more cheaply than you'd expect, because two of the three pieces already exist.

## Why it's possible

Keycloak renders that page, but **you already ship a custom login theme for it**: `infrastructure/keycloak/themes/account-user/`, wired to the `account-app` client via `login_theme`. And that theme already calls your API — `posts.js` fetches `/api/public/posts` to draw the announcements column beside the form.

So the question isn't "can we change the page", it's "can the page know which club". It can, from its own URL. Clicking Sign in on the Meath gateway sends the browser to:

```
…/protocol/openid-connect/auth?client_id=account-app
  &redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A5176%2Faccount%2Fmhpc
  &code_challenge=…
```

`mhpc` is right there. And `GET /api/public/organisations/mhpc` is anonymous and returns `displayName: "Meath Hunt Pony Club"` — I checked, 200 without a token. Same fetch pattern the theme already uses.

## The one thing that would break a naive version

I tested it rather than assuming. Enter a **wrong password** and Keycloak re-renders at:

```
…/login-actions/authenticate?execution=…&client_id=account-app&tab_id=CScbOBpPVt0
```

**No `redirect_uri`.** A script that just reads the URL would show the club name, then lose it the moment someone mistypes their password — the worst possible moment.

The fix is small: stash the code in `sessionStorage` on first render. That page is Keycloak's own origin, so it survives the re-render in the same tab. Worth knowing up front, because it's the difference between this working and looking broken.

## What `client.name` can't do

The obvious server-side answer — `${client.name}` in the template — doesn't work here, because all four clubs share one `account-app` client. It would say "account-app" for everyone.

## The alternatives, honestly

| Approach | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Theme JS + `redirect_uri`** | ~40 lines in the existing theme, no new infrastructure. Needs the sessionStorage detail above |
| **A Keycloak client per organisation** | `${client.name}` server-side, no JS at all. But N clients to create and keep in step, the account app must pick one per club, and the token audience changes per club |
| **Keycloak Organizations (`kc_org`)** | Purpose-built for exactly this — and it's Keycloak 26. You're on **23.0.7**, so it's a major upgrade away |
| **Custom Authenticator SPI** | The "proper" server-side route: a Java extension setting a form attribute. A jar to build, deploy and version alongside Keycloak |

## What I'd do

The theme-JS route. It reuses the theme you already have and the public endpoint you already have, and the failure mode is benign — the existing `posts.js` already establishes the rule that everything on that page is wrapped so a failed fetch leaves the panel empty and never touches the sign-in form. Worst case you get today's page.

One caution if we do it: the club name must go in with `textContent`, never `innerHTML`. It arrives via a URL parameter, so it's attacker-controllable, and the login page is the one page where an injection matters most.

Want me to build it? I'd add it to `account-user/login/template.ftl` with its own small script, and check it in the browser at both moments — first load, and after a deliberately wrong password.

## How it knows

**A wrong password loses `redirect_uri`.** Keycloak re-renders at `/login-actions/authenticate?execution=…&tab_id=…`, and the parameter is gone. A URL-only script would name the club on the first attempt and drop it the instant someone mistyped — the worst moment for a sign-in page to look unsure where it is. |---|---|

| Unknown club code | Line hidden; form and password field untouched |

## Two decisions worth knowing

**No fallback to the code.** If the name can't be fetched the line stays away rather than reading "Signing in to mhpc", which tells a member less than silence and reads as a fault.

**`%organisation%`, not `{0}`.** My first attempt used `{organisation}` and Keycloak returned a 500: every theme message goes through Java's `MessageFormat`, which claims anything in braces — `can't parse argument number: organisation`. The name goes in with `textContent`, never `innerHTML` — it originates in a public URL parameter, and this is the page where an injection would be worth mounting.

## The part that's correct

`listPayments` deliberately excludes unpaid payments:

```sql
WHERE p.user_id = $1 AND p.organisation_id = $2
  AND p.payment_status NOT IN ('pending', 'abandoned')
```

A member's payment history is money that **moved**. That Ward entry is offline — the money reaches the club in person — so until someone records it, there's nothing to list. It says so on the entry, which is where it belongs.

## The part that was wrong, and it's mine

**The seed created no payments at all.** Zero rows, every account, every club. So the page was empty everywhere — for paid purchases too. The awaiting-payment entry just made it noticeable.

That's a hole I put there. In this system an entry *cannot* exist without a payment: `checkout.service` writes a `payments` row and a `payment_transactions` line per basket item, and only then does `fulfilment.service` write the `event_entries` row. Seeding entries directly produced a state the application can't reach — two screens disagreeing about one purchase, with no bug to find. Same for memberships, which are also bought through a basket.

## Fixed

Every seeded entry and membership now writes the payment behind it, shaped the way checkout shapes one — `payment_type: 'cart'`, the fee in major units on `payments` and minor on the transaction, the entry's own method and status, `payment_date` only where money moved, the `offline_amount`/`card_amount` split, and `fulfilled_at` on paid lines. **72 payments and 72 transactions** across 38 entries and 34 memberships.

A refunded membership gets a *refunded* payment rather than none — the money did move, and a history omitting it is the one shape a member would query.

## One more entry, for the case you found

Niamh at Ward was the **only** login-and-club pair whose single purchase was the unpaid one, so even after the fix her Ward Payments page stayed empty — correct, and still indistinguishable from broken. She now has a second Ward entry that's paid:

```

Ward Union Open Day — Family ticket              paid      (on both)
```

That pair is worth keeping — the difference between those two rows *is* the answer to your question. A test holds the general rule: every login has at least one paid purchase in every club it belongs to.

Here's what the seed configures. Both fees are set on the **organisation type** (`irish-pony-clubs`), and only ever on the card method — `pay-offline` gets nulls for both.

## Handling fee — what the member pays

One setting, inherited by all four clubs, no per-club override anywhere in the seed:

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Fixed | **€0.25** per card payment |
| Percentage | **1.5%** of the fee-bearing base |
| Tax on the fee | **0%** |

Three rules govern how that lands, and the seed exercises all of them:

- The percentage applies to the **fee-bearing base**, not the card subtotal — an item whose price already absorbs its handling fee is excluded, or the member is billed twice.
- The fixed €0.25 is charged **once per payment**, not per item.
- **No fee-bearing items means no fee at all**, fixed element included. That's why Áine's basket 2 comes to €67.00 with €0.00 fee.

Worked example from the seed — basket 1, two card entries at €25 and €30, both fee-added-on: €0.25 + 1.5% of €55 = €1.075 → **€1.08**, split €0.49 / €0.59 by largest remainder.

## Application fee — the platform's cut from the club

Type default **€0.30 + 1.5%**, then copied onto each organisation at creation, exactly as the admin UI does. Two clubs diverge, deliberately, so that copy-on-create is visible without editing anything:

| Club | Card methods | Application fee |
|---|---|---|
| Kildare Hunt PC | offline + stripe | €0.30 + 1.5% *(type default)* |
| Laois Hunt PC | offline + stripe | **€0.15 + 1.0%** — overridden |
| Ward Union PC | offline only | **null / null** — no card method, so nothing to charge |
| Meath Hunt PC | offline + stripe | €0.30 + 1.5% *(type default)* |

Ward Union is worth noting: it isn't "zero", it's **null** — the club has no card method switched on at all, so there's no card payment for a platform share to be taken from.

## Two things to keep straight

**Units differ between the two.** `handlingFee.fixedFee` is written in major units (0.25 = €0.25) and read back in minor units by `organizationTypePaymentFeeService` — that conversion is why the seed does `Math.round(fixedFee * 100)` when computing basket fees. `percentageFee: 1.5` means 1.5%, not 150%.

**They're unrelated to the Stripe Connect accounts.** Those are created per club (`acct_…`) but carry no fee configuration — the numbers above all live in `organization_type_payment_fees` and `organization_payment_application_fees` in your own database, not in Stripe.

## How the membership survives the journey

Renewal spans three screens — the card, the catalogue, the form. The card knows which membership; the form is where it matters; nothing connected them. The id now travels as `?renew=`:

```
/khpc/memberships                                    Renew
/khpc/browse/memberships?renew=member-9              choose a type
/khpc/browse/memberships/mt-1/apply?renew=member-9   form opens filled in
```

**Deliberately not inferred server-side** from "their most recent membership of that type". A parent holds four, and guessing would eventually open the form with the wrong child's details — a wrong answer that looks like the member's own.

## Where the answers come from

New `GET /:orgCode/memberships/:id/form-answers` returns the stored `submission_data`, keyed by field `name` — the same shape the form already holds its values in, so the prefill is a merge rather than a translation. Scoped to the caller's own memberships, with not-found and not-yours answering identically: it returns the contents of an application form, so confirming an id is real would leak which ids exist.

## Three rules

- **Only fields the chosen type asks for.** Renewing into a *different* type is allowed and that type may ask different questions; an answer to a question nobody asked would be submitted as an orphan.
- **Fills blanks, never overwrites.** Anything already typed stays.
- **A failure leaves a working form.** If the answers can't be read it opens blank — exactly as before. A convenience mustn't be able to take the form down with it.

## One thing I added that you didn't ask for

> *Filled in from your current membership. Please check it is still correct.*

A form that fills itself in has to be checked. Without knowing where the answers came from, a member either trusts them unread — and renews on an address they've moved out of — or retypes them anyway, which is the work this saves. Easy to drop if you'd rather it were silent.

## Verified

"Confirming your payment..."

However after about 30 seconds, the screen changes and it shows "Confirming your order" with the mesage underneath "Your payment is being confirmed. This page will update shortly." but ot never does and the item still shows in my backet with the option to Checkout again ?

Can you fix this ?

### Assistant

Only the webhook can confirm a payment. Let me see what we know about the Stripe side:

The intent id **is** stored at checkout. Let me confirm the diagnosis against your actual database before building anything:

Stripe says **`requires_capture`** — the money is authorised but never captured. Let me see what handles that:

Now I have the full chain. Let me check how the webhook service is wired, since that's where settle+confirm+fulfil already meet:

Now the reconcile itself, in the service that already coordinates settle, confirm and fulfil:

Now wire it into the endpoint the confirmation page already polls:

Now let me prove it against your actual stuck payment:

Two passes, as designed. Let me verify what it produced downstream:

Payment paid, cart closed, membership created. Now tests:

Fixed — and your stuck payment is now settled.

## What was actually wrong

Your payment was still `pending` in the database. Asking Stripe directly:

```
pi_3UAp4B2lw1vfQg8P1Z84xz43  →  requires_capture   7670 eur   received 0
```

**`requires_capture`, not `succeeded`.** Card payments here are taken in two steps — authorise at checkout, capture once the order is confirmed still available — and yours was authorised and never captured.

Both steps are driven by webhooks, and `confirmPayment` and `settleAuthorisation` had exactly **one caller between them**: the webhook service. So with no webhook, nothing could move the payment on. Stripe can't reach your laptop without `stripe listen --forward-to …`.

The confirmation screen wasn't broken — it polls ten times over twenty seconds and reports what the server says. The server was telling the truth; the truth was that the payment was stuck.

## The fix: ask, rather than wait to be told

`webhookService.reconcilePayment()` brings a payment up to date from the provider's own view, and the status endpoint calls it whenever the payment is still pending or authorised:

| Stripe says | What happens |
|---|---|
| `requires_capture` | settle it — captures the money |
| `succeeded` | confirm it, close the cart, fulfil it |
| `canceled` | fail it, with a reason |
| in flight (3-D Secure) or unreachable | nothing |

**Two passes, not one** — settling captures, and capture is what makes Stripe say `succeeded`; the next poll two seconds later confirms. Guessing the capture worked would be the same mistake in reverse. Well inside the 20-second budget.

Every step is the code the webhook already runs and every step is idempotent, so a webhook arriving mid-reconcile changes nothing. Anything already paid, refunded, failed or abandoned is never re-opened — the provider isn't even asked. And reconciling can't fail the request: an unreachable Stripe mustn't turn a slow confirmation into an error page.

## Proved on your actual payment

```
BEFORE:  pending
pass 1 → settled    payment now authorised
pass 2 → paid       payment now paid

payment: paid, 10:45:03      cart: ordered      line: membership | fulfilled
```

Payment settled, **basket closed**, **membership created** — the three things that hadn't happened. Go and look; it should be in your memberships now.

## Worth knowing

Webhooks stay the primary path and are untouched — this is the safety net under them. It happens to make local card payments work without `stripe listen`, but it also covers the worst failure this system has in production: money taken, nothing delivered, and no way out but a manual database fix.

Backend: 177 suites, **3357 tests**, typecheck clean. 19 new tests across the service and the endpoint.

Now the fixes. First, the root cause — this router never told the audit trail which club it was acting for:

Now let the `audited()` middleware see the response when composing an action's values:

Now the two routes — a distinct action for the undo, plus a label and a record of what happened:

Now the label test and the full backend/typecheck run:

Fixed — the record was being written, but three things kept it out of your log.

## Why you couldn't see it

The event existed in `audit_events` all along. It was written with **`organisation_id = NULL`**, and the org-admin audit log filters on exactly that.

`audited()` scopes an event from `req.organisationId`, which `organisation-scope.middleware` sets on every router that takes the club from the URL. [orgadmin-organisation.routes.ts](packages/backend/src/routes/orgadmin-organisation.routes.ts) is the exception — it resolves the club itself from your token plus `X-Organisation-Id`, and kept the answer in a local variable. `withOrganisation` now puts it on the request, which fixes **every** audited route on that router at once: payment settings, branding, email templates, registration settings and the approval queue, not just these two. The settings routes had been escaping it by accident — they PUT the whole organisation, so the id was findable in the request body. An empty POST has nowhere to look.

I backfilled the one receipt already in your database (the Meath one, `695b04c7…`), so it now shows in that club's log.

## Making the message clear

**A receipt and its undo were the same action.** Both wrote `offline-payment.recorded`, so a reversal read identically to the thing it reversed. The DELETE now writes `offline-payment.receipt-undone` — registered in `AUDIT_ACTIONS`, labelled in [auditLabels.ts](packages/components/src/utils/auditLabels.ts), translated in all six locales. `offline-payment.recorded` is relabelled *"Offline payment recorded as received"*; "recorded" alone reads as the checkout rather than the settlement.

**The entry said nothing.** It was `changes: {"created": {}}` with no label — somebody did something to a uuid. Both routes take an empty body, and the middleware records what was *sent*; what matters here is in the reply. So `audited()`'s `values` composer now also receives the response:

```ts
values?: (req: Request, after: Record<string, unknown> | null) => Record<string, unknown> | null;
```

Backwards compatible (every existing caller ignores the second argument), and `null` on the failure path. The two routes now produce:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Label** | `Fionn Doyle — EUR 45.00`, falling back to the email where no name is recorded |
| **Changes** | Payer, Amount, Currency, Payment status, Received at, and for a receipt **Items created / Items failed** |

`itemsFailed` earns its place: a half-successful settlement is announced once in an alert the administrator may close, and after that the trail is the only thing that remembers. A refused undo — one whose receipt has already produced memberships — is recorded as a `failure` carrying the refusal reason.

Six new tests in [orgadmin-offline-payments.routes.test.ts](packages/backend/src/routes/__tests__/orgadmin-offline-payments.routes.test.ts) (the organisation on the event, the money and fulfilment outcome in `changes`, the label and its email fallback, the undo as its own action, a refused undo as a failure) and three in [audit.middleware.test.ts](packages/backend/src/middleware/__tests__/audit.middleware.test.ts) for the widened `values`. ## The four scopes

They're not four ways of typing a number — the difference decides what the payment becomes, so the dialog sends a **scope**, not a figure:

| Scope | Amount | Payment becomes |
|---|---|---|
| Whole payment | everything still refundable | `refunded` |
| All but the handling fee | everything bar what the card cost | `refunded` |
| Particular items | the chosen lines, at what was paid for each | `partially_refunded` → `refunded` once the parts cover it |
| Another amount | what was typed, capped at what's left | as above |

**The server computes the amount for every scope but the last.** A client able to name both a scope and a figure could refund the whole of a payment while calling it one line of it, and the status would follow the label rather than the money.

**A judgement call you should check:** I made *"all but the handling fee"* settle the payment as `refunded` rather than leaving it partially refunded. You listed only options 3 and 4 as partial, and the reasoning is that the fee is what the card cost the club — added on top of the price, not part of it — so a club that has returned everything it took for the goods has refunded the order. Say the word if you'd rather it read as partial. It's offered **only where a fee was added on**; a basket whose prices absorb their fee has none to keep back, and asking for it there is refused rather than being a full refund under another name.

A line refunds at its own fee **plus its share of the handling fee** — the member paid both.

## Repeatable, ending at Refunded

`partially_refunded` is as refundable as `paid`. Each refund records what it covered in a new `refund_transactions` table, so an item already refunded isn't offered again (and is refused if asked for), a part-refunded line can go back up to what's left, and when the parts cover the payment it becomes `refunded`. Verified end-to-end against your real Kildare basket:

```
items refund (Áine's 80cm, €25.62)  → partially_refunded, 1 entry withdrawn
€10 goodwill                        → partially_refunded  (€35.62 back)
the rest                            → refunded            (€185.23 back)
one more                            → refused: "Can only refund paid payments"
same item twice                     → refused: "That item has already been refunded"
```

## Withdrawing the entries

Asked, never assumed — a refund can be a goodwill gesture with the rider still expected. The checkbox says what it means, and appears only when the refund actually covers entries.

`entry_status = 'removed'` with `removed_at`, `removed_by`, `removal_reason` — not a delete, and not a `deleted` flag: the entry happened, was paid for and was refunded. What changes is where it appears: **off the entrant list**, **out of every capacity count** (event list, account catalogue, public listings — a withdrawn entry mustn't hold a place), still on its own page under *"This entry was withdrawn on…"*, and chipped **€25.62 refunded** / **Entry withdrawn** on the payment's items table.

Never for an arbitrary amount that leaves the payment short — €20 off a basket of four names no item, and picking entries would invent a decision the club didn't make. Only `event_entry` lines; silently cancelling a membership or booking off the back of a refund is a different conversation.

## Also worth knowing

- **`{ refundAmount }` with no scope is treated as an amount refund**, not as "everything". Defaulting to full there would ignore the figure sent and refund the whole payment — the one mistake here that moves more money than was asked for.
- Migration `1709000000039` (run on your dev and test databases), and I brought your existing seeded refunds into line: the three partial ones now read `partially_refunded`.
- `partially_refunded` added to the list filter, both chips (amber — money has gone back and some hasn't), and the member-facing status in the account app.

For this order, http://localhost:5175/orgadmin/payments/554355d4-dfc1-4d5c-8380-8b88c92899e3 in the displayed details page it is showing Partially refunded, and the refund section at the end of the page is showing that the Show Cap was refunded, however in the section titled "What This Paid For" it is still showing the "Show Cap" as "Paid" and not Refunded"

Also, one of the items in a payment was refunded, and when I selected to do a second refund, the pop up dialog was displayed and when I clicked Particular Item, it allowed me to select the item that had prevously been refunded, can you fix this so the Particular item list only shows items that have not already been refunded.

### Assistant

Now the dialog's second guard — the selected items must fit inside what's left:

Both had one cause, and it wasn't the status column.

## What was actually wrong

That refund is **seeded** data: written with `scope: 'amount'`, €18.00, and a reason that *mentions* the cap — *"Cap ordered in the wrong size"*. Nothing linked it to the Show cap line. So each screen was telling the truth about a different thing:

- the refund section read the **reason**, which names the cap;
- the status column read the **money**, and no money was recorded against that line;
- the item list saw a line with nothing refunded against it, so it offered it again.

The status column was right. The data was wrong.

## The fix

The fixture now names the item, and the writer links it:

```ts
{ basket: 'mcnamara-day',   item: { description: 'Show cap' },                        … }
{ basket: 'mcgrath-season', item: { description: '80cm', subject: 'Rónán McGrath' },  … }
```

- **Exactly one line must match, or the seed refuses to run** — a fixture that quietly matched none would write the very state you just hit.
- **The entrant, where the description isn't enough.** Two children in the same class produce two identical lines; `subject` reads `context_ref.entrantName`, which is how it tells Rónán's €25.61 line from Áine's €25.62.
- **The amount comes from the line** — its fee plus the share of the handling fee it bore — rather than being restated in the fixture. So the cap refund is **€18.44**, not the €18.00 the fixture claimed.
- Written with scope `items` and a `refund_transactions` row.

I repaired the three already in your database rather than leaving them. That payment now reads:

```
payment partially_refunded  €99.29
   Tara Hunter Trial — Open class             paid        refunded=0.00
   Horse registration 2026 — Ballinteer Boy   paid        refunded=0.00
   Show cap — One size                        refunded    refunded=18.44
   refund €18.44 items → Show cap — One size

   items offered for a second refund: Tara Hunter Trial | Horse registration 2026
```

## A second guard on the dialog

Selecting items that add up to more than the payment has left is now refused in the dialog rather than by the server. That's reachable **without** any of the chosen items having been refunded: an earlier arbitrary-amount refund comes off the payment without naming a line, so the lines can still total more than remains.

## Tests

Green: backend **180 suites / 3445**, orgadmin-core **57 files / 951**. New: two seed-fixture rules (no part refund may name an amount instead of an item; an ambiguous class description must also name the entrant) and the dialog's over-total guard. Verified by seeding a scratch database — three linked refunds, correct amounts — and against your live payment. [PARTIAL_REFUNDS.md](docs/PARTIAL_REFUNDS.md) has the write-up.

One caveat on the first full backend run: it reported 1 failure, and two subsequent runs were clean at 3445. I didn't capture which suite, so I can't tell you whether it was the flaky offline-payments one CLAUDE.md notes or a race with the scratch database I was dropping at the time — worth an eye if it shows up again.

### Assistant

Now `useApi` — the reason the screen said "Undone":

Now the Mark Received / Undo buttons on the payment detail:

Verifying the undo against the payment that failed for you:

The audit trail told the story your screen wouldn't:

```
15:43  offline-payment.receipt-undone   failure
14:52  offline-payment.receipt-undone   failure
14:52  offline-payment.receipt-undone   failure
14:50  offline-payment.recorded         success
```

Three refusals, reported to you as three successes. Two separate defects.

## 1. `useApi.execute` answers `null` instead of throwing

Every `try { await execute(...) } catch` around a mutation in this codebase is **dead code**. The hook records the message in its own state and resolves to `null`; the catch never fires and the page runs its success path. The module summary already documented this trap for *loads* — it's the same trap on the write path, and worse there, because a refusal reads as "done".

Changing the default would touch ~240 call sites that read the `null`, so it's opt-in: `throwOnError: true`, which throws the server's own words. Applied to mark-received, undo, and the new buttons.

## 2. The undo refused what the receipt hadn't created

It counted **everything the payment had ever produced**. But an entry, a booking and a merchandise order are created *when the order is placed* — deliberately, so a member isn't without their entry while a cheque is in the post. On your payment the line was fulfilled on **24 August** and the receipt was **1 September**: it released nothing, and the undo was refused for records it never made. That made Undo a permanent lie for almost every offline order there is.

It now counts only `fulfilled_at >= offline_received_at` — what *this receipt* released. A membership or registration, the two fulfilment defers, still blocks it, which is the case the rule exists for, and the message says so: *"Recording this payment created memberships, bookings or orders."*

Verified on the payment that failed for you:

```
line: event_entry fulfilled 2026-08-24 — before any receipt
marked received: paid, released 0
undone:          awaiting_offline, received —
back on the Outstanding list? true
```

One thing I can't explain: a fourth attempt at 15:50 *succeeded* under the old rule, which is why that payment is currently sitting in Outstanding. I don't want to guess at the sequence.

## Mark Received / Undo on the payment detail

Both now sit beside Request Refund, calling the same two endpoints. **Mark received** appears on `awaiting_offline` — the same status the Offline Payments screen selects on, so the two agree about what's outstanding. **Undo** appears whenever there's an `offline_received_at`; whether it's *allowed* is the server's call, so the button is offered and the refusal shown in its own words. A partial fulfilment comes back as a warning, not a tick.

## The settlement history you asked for is already there

Built in the earlier round: the **Offline settlement** card, below "What this paid for" — who marked it received or undid it, when, and what the receipt released. It's populated for that payment (`received · Deirdre Ó Ceallaigh`). It shows successes only; the three refusals live in the audit log under Failures. If you're not seeing it, the dev backend likely predates that change.

In the seed program can you add a set of ticket based entries, so I can see the functionality in action.

### Assistant

Now the fixture — a past ticketed event whose tickets have been through the gate:

Now the past ticketed event and its entries:

Now the writer — issuing the tickets and their scan history:

Now the fixture tests:

The seed configured one event for tickets and issued **none** — so the whole module had nothing to show.

## Two ticketed events now, not one

A ticket is written for **every entry on a ticketing event**, because that's what the app does (`fulfilment.service` → `issueTicketForEntry`). The fixture doesn't ask for a ticket; it says what happened to it afterwards.

```
Electronic tickets
  Dunshaughlin Gate Day (completed)  Meath Hunt Pony Club     6 issued, 4 scanned
  Tara Hunter Trial                  Meath Hunt Pony Club     5 issued, 0 scanned
```

**A completed event was the missing half.** Every ticketed event in the fixture was in the future, and a scan dated in the future is a state a gate can't produce — so there was no honest way to show scanning at all. *Dunshaughlin Gate Day*, twelve days ago at Meath, now carries it:

| Entrant | | |
|---|---|---|
| Bríd McNamara, Colm Fitzgerald | `scanned` | admitted at the Main gate |
| **Éabha O'Toole** | `scannedTwice` | presented twice — `scan_count` 2, two rows in its history |
| Séamus Donnelly | `issued` | paid and never came |
| Maeve Kiernan | `cancelled` | withdrew, so the ticket was cancelled |
| Aoibhínn Regan | `scanned` | at the Junior ring — the location isn't always the same |

Written the way the service writes one: the reference from the same sequence (so seeded and app-issued tickets can't collide), validity from the start of the event *day* to the last day plus the configured period, and **every** scan in the history rather than only the last — that's what makes a duplicate visible.

## Two disagreements I found and did not silently fix

**`ticket_validity_period` contradicts its own label.** The service adds it to the event's last day — *days, afterwards*. The form labels it **"Ticket Validity Period (hours)"** and its help text says *hours before the event start*. Unit and direction both differ: a club entering 24 meaning "valid from yesterday" gets a ticket valid 24 extra days. The fixture follows the code (Tara's 24 became 1) because that's what the data will look like; changing either side moves the validity of tickets already issued, so that's your call.

**`scanResult` has two vocabularies.** The front-end type declares `'valid' | 'invalid' | 'already_scanned' | 'expired'`; the backend only ever writes `'success'`. Nothing breaks — the dialog prints it raw — but the type describes a set the API never produces, and a duplicate is told by the count, not the result.

## In your database now

I issued the five missing tickets for the existing Tara Hunter Trial entries **through `issueTicketForEntry` itself**, so the module isn't empty before you reseed. The gate day — and with it every scan, the duplicate and the cancellation — needs `npm run seed:demo`.

## Tests

Backend green: **180 suites / 3453**. Six new fixture rules: a ticketed event in the past *and* one to come, every ticketed event has entries, a ticket state only where tickets are issued, all four states covered, scans only on an event that has happened, and every ticketed entry made before its event ran. Verified against a scratch database — 11 tickets, 5 scan-history rows, the duplicate showing as two. All three now produce real workbooks. Now the tests that were hiding it:
